title: Vishal Dadlani Called Her Singing 'Embarrassing for the Country.' Eighteen Months Later, He Apologised on National Television.
excerpt: The Coldplay India feud that split the music industry finally got its reckoning — on the Indian Idol stage, with Jasleen Royal sitting right there.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Vishal Dadlani apologized to Jasleen Royal on *Indian Idol* for past derogatory comments.
  • Jasleen was the first Indian solo artist to open for Coldplay in India, facing immense pressure.
  • The incident highlighted tensions between traditional and modern Indian music representation.
  • Jasleen's streaming success contrasts with the industry's preference for classically trained artists.
  • The apology marks a rare admission of fault in Bollywood's competitive music scene.
It took eighteen months and a television set to get the words out. But on Saturday's episode of *Indian Idol*, **Vishal Dadlani** — one half of the Vishal-Shekhar powerhouse, the man who scored *Om Shanti Om* and *Chennai Express*, the judge whose opinions arrive without a safety net — turned to **Jasleen Royal** and apologised on national television for calling her Coldplay opening act "embarrassing." > "I said more than I should have on the issue, and I shouldn't have. My mistake was that I wanted to blame the organisers somewhere, but I expressed it the wrong way." — Vishal Dadlani The apology closed a chapter that has quietly haunted India's music industry since January 2025, when Coldplay's *Music of the Spheres* tour swept through Mumbai's DY Patil Stadium for a series of concerts that became the biggest live-music event in Indian history. Jasleen Royal — the self-taught artist behind *Heeriye*, *Ranjha*, and the *Kho Gaye Hum Kahan* soundtrack — was handpicked to open the show. She was the first Indian solo artist to open for Coldplay on home soil, and the pressure was enormous. ## The Instagram Story That Refused to Die ![Jasleen Royal — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0c/Jasleen_Royal_performing_in_Rajasthan_%28cropped%29.jpg) Within hours of the Mumbai concerts, Vishal posted a now-deleted Instagram story that never named Jasleen but left little room for misinterpretation. "When you put a basic-to-bad singer in front of a large crowd on a large stage, all you're doing is showing more people that the individual can't really sing," he wrote. "How embarrassing! For the country, the artiste, the public, as well as 'the scene.'" The post disappeared from his feed, but the internet had already screenshotted it into permanence. Reddit threads on r/BollyBlindsNGossip dissected the remarks within hours. Fellow playback singer **Antara Mitra** piled on with her own Instagram story, calling it a "numbers game, not music" and adding that "someone from the same field should call this out." > **"I don't want people to think that she didn't deserve to be here," she said in the documentary."** The pile-on was brutal. Fans of Jasleen pointed out that she had been personally invited by **Chris Martin**. That she had performed *We Pray* with him onstage. That she had walked into a 50,000-strong crowd — most of them there for a British band, not an Indian opener — and still showed up. Critics countered that an event of that magnitude demanded a Shreya Ghoshal or a Sunidhi Chauhan, not an artist whose strengths are intimate, studio-built records. ## What It Did to Jasleen In a mini-documentary that surfaced months after the concerts, Jasleen revealed she had broken down backstage after reading the backlash. She was seen hugging her parents, visibly shaken. ![Chennai — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Chennai_Central.jpg) "I am nervous. I don't want people to think that she didn't deserve to be here," she said in the documentary. "I am a self-taught musician. So, I know I am not perfect. I keep learning every day. I try to better myself every day. But I try to put up a great show where people have a great experience." Before her second-day performance, she addressed the crowd directly — acknowledging her nerves, thanking those who had shown faith. The vulnerability was disarming. ## The Apology — and Jasleen's Response Saturday's *Indian Idol* moment finally brought the two face to face on camera. Vishal's apology was measured but unequivocal: he had aimed his frustration at the event's organisers for what he saw as a curatorial mismatch, but the words had landed squarely on the artist.
The Coldplay India Controversy
January 2025
Coldplay's *Music of the Spheres* tour begins in Mumbai.
January 2025
Jasleen Royal opens for Coldplay, becoming the first Indian solo artist to do so.
Hours after concert
Vishal Dadlani posts critical Instagram story about Jasleen's performance.
Months later
Jasleen shares her emotional response in a mini-documentary.
Recent *Indian Idol* episode
Vishal publicly apologizes to Jasleen for his comments.
![Mumbai — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2b/Mumbai_Bandra-Worli_Sea_Link.jpg) Jasleen's response was equally telling. "I see you as a mentor and a friend," she told him, "so it hurt me." That single line carried more weight than any Instagram clapback could. It reframed the entire episode from a public takedown into a private betrayal between two people who knew each other in the small world of Indian music. ## The Bigger Question for Indian Music The Coldplay controversy was never just about one opening act. It was about who gets to represent Indian music on the world stage — and who gets to decide that. The Coldplay India tour was the first time global pop infrastructure collided with India's own star system at this scale, and it exposed a fault line: between artists built by streaming algorithms and those who came up through the classical-playback ecosystem. Jasleen Royal's numbers are undeniable — *Heeriye* alone has crossed a billion streams. But the industry's old guard, raised on rigorous vocal training and film-studio hierarchy, has never fully accepted that streaming success and stage presence are the same thing. Vishal's original critique, however clumsily delivered, was about that gap.

The apology doesn't resolve the debate. But it does something rarer in Bollywood's ego-driven ecosystem: it admits fault, on camera, without a publicist's hand forcing it. In an industry where beefs simmer for decades and grudges outlast careers, that counts for something. For the diaspora — many of whom were in those DY Patil crowds, having flown in from London and New Jersey and Toronto specifically for the shows — the episode is a reminder that Indian music's growing pains are playing out in real time. The stages are getting bigger. The question of who belongs on them is only getting louder.
